speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There has also been greater emphasis on whole-of-Government coordination and no-wrong-door access for public enquiries and requests for service.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides MSO, officers in the Public Service, especially those doing front-line work, should be equipped with the right skills and competencies to deliver good service.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, there should be developmental opportunities for service staff so that they can acquire and broaden their capabilities and be specialists in these areas.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With rising expectations on the Public Service to better serve Singaporeans, how is the Public Service Division preparing public officers to help them continue to deliver quality services and continually seek to improve their service delivery?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a recognisable training and competency framework targeted at enhancing service delivery?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the officers look forward to clear career progression pathways for service-related and frontline jobs within the Public Service?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there also plans to leverage technology to spearhead innovative service initiatives to augment service delivery format?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also want to urge the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) to continue with its efforts to protect our officers from abuse and unfair treatment meted out to them by the public.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The few offending members of the public can cause great distress to the officers and further delay others from receiving the same type of services.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must do our best for a more cordial engagement between our Public Service officers and members of the public.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Because it is a patient, the burden is placed on nurses, that we are supposed to "take it in our stride", that we ought to be long-suffering in these matters.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Imagine how this would play out in the social media if a nurse had tried to defend herself physically against an attacker.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we must bear in mind that physical abuse by anyone is not acceptable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This same asymmetry applies to the poor, the needy, residents and anyone, indeed, whom the public officers are trying to help.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They are the customers and they are always right.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What does that say about our patients and the family of our patients?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Being sick does not entitle one to be violent or disrespectful.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But how many nurses can say this to their patients?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, the public servants cannot be ignored.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to continue identifying, assessing and mitigate the factors that lead to abuse, to bring about a safe workplace for our public officers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Public Service is the backbone of the provision of all services to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should respect public servants and protect them from abuse or harassment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Other than criminally prosecuting the perpetrators, I feel that non-confrontational styles of approach can be taught to Public Service workers to respond adequately to these occurrences before they turn into offences.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Have we trained staff to recognise early stages of occurrences and alert them to potentially abusive intent?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Are staff already trained in any security measures or devices to alert fellow workers?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I know there are closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras installed in many places now, partly to provide monitoring capabilities, but also to provide evidence for "just in case" moments.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In many places, CCTVs are now the bastion between behaving decently and terribly.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have no policy fixes, and CCTVs or body worn cameras are a poor substitute for basic courtesy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But if they are necessary and they help the public officials, I say, go ahead, let us have more of them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What else can be done to support their needs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I can see the merits of outsourcing and the hiving off of engineering units as private entities, I believe the Public Service still needs to retain a high level of engineering capabilities and core competencies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether it is in the administering of engineering projects, contract management, regulation, technical grants allocation or even policymaking with regard to very technical areas, such as automation and robotics, the Public Service clearly needs to possess key domain expertise to carry out the functions of the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government must never be in a position where it is overly dependent on the private sector for engineering advice and loses its ability to do internal engineering appraisals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to attract and recruit more engineers into the Public Service and to ensure that the fresh cohorts of younger engineers continue to be inducted to succeed the retiring engineers so as to strengthen the organic capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Anecdotally, when I interact with many public sector engineers, it seems that there are more white-hair engineers now.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It seems that the professional engineers in the public sector are ageing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would like to make a special mention of two very competent and experienced senior engineers that I have the pleasure of working with in the Government Parliamentary Committee for the Environment and in my constituency work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are Mr Tan Nguan Sen and Mr Yap Kheng Guan from the Public Utilities Board (PUB).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Both men and many other engineers in PUB epitomise the passion and competency of PUB engineers as well as the deep expertise they have on how to sustain Singapore's self-sufficiency in water resource.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is always a reassuring experience whenever I seek assistance from both of them on constituency-related engineering problems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They show deep knowledge and experience on PUB-related matters and will always offer good practical solutions to local problems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that the Public Service continues to bring about such passionate, resolute and capable engineers to the ranks and inculcate in them the pioneer values and the can-do spirit to turn our vulnerability or whatever adversity we encounter into strengths.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How is the Public Service growing its engineering capabilities and developing its engineering workforce in the years to come?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are there fulfilling career paths for public sector engineers and are they competitively compensated?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given that the Public Service has outsourced and already privatised many of its engineering activities in the past, will there be sufficient engineering jobs in the public sector and where are the areas of growth?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Top science students either studied medicine or engineering.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of my seniors proudly told me their contribution and involvement in our nation-building.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As Singapore enters the next lap of its nationhood, do we still have passionate and committed engineers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We will need many computer engineers and information technology (IT) experts to make us a Smart Nation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need engineers to keep our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) system, airport and seaport working in tip-top conditions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need engineers to build smarter homes, clean supply of water and even security system for protection of our country.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do we have enough engineers to bring our nation to the next level?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our engineering faculties are unable to attract enough locals and have to fill the vacancies with foreign students.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, one local student was joking: whenever he says that he is from engineering, he has to quickly specify he is Singaporean, otherwise people will assume he is a foreigner.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, there is the perception that studying engineering is boring and tough.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Those engineers who have accountant, lawyer or doctor wives told me that their wives earn more than them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many also feel being an engineer is tough.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Not only do they have to spend long hours in their job, there is also the feeling that when things go wrong, everybody blames the engineers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, there is a saying: a scientist can fail all his life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He just needs to have one success to win the Nobel Prize.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Whereas engineers you have to do it right all your life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To maximise the Government's efforts, I urge the Government to also influence the private sector through the contracts it awards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also hope the Deputy Prime Minister will look at the career progression of engineers, both current and future, in the public sector and beyond, and how we can upgrade them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to ensure that the public sector is able to attract and retain the best engineering and technology capability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is critical in giving the increasing role that technology is playing in all aspects of our economy, society and life, and our focus towards a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What efforts and plans does the public sector have to ensure we have both the skills base and capacity to support the transformation of Singapore towards a Smart Nation?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Public Service has continually reviewed and reorganised itself to be ready for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is headed by the Head of Civil Service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Its role is to identify emerging priorities early and tackle medium- to long-term issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Strategy Group looks at the impact of future trends on our external and domestic environment, the policies we might need, and the capabilities we need to build in Government to address the challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These changes allow the Public Service to develop and deliver better policies, services and programmes for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee asked about our efforts to deliver good services to citizens.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our public agencies have made progress in working together to serve Singaporeans better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, the 24 Social Services Offices (SSOs) under the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) partner other public agencies to offer integrated services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Members would know that when a family needs temporary financial help, housing rental assistance and employment assistance, they can go to the nearest SSO, which will coordinate with the Workforce Developement Agency and the Housing and Development Board (HDB) to provide this help in a holistic way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the Ministry of National Development's (MND's) Committee of Supply debate, Members were updated about the work of the MSO to improve the coordination and delivery of municipal services across public agencies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Ministry of Finance also highlighted recent e-initiatives by several Ministries during its COS debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will continue to use technology more effectively to enhance the delivery of Government services, for example, by making more services available online and on mobile platforms, so that they are accessible at any time, from anywhere.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This recently has been tax-filing season, and many Members would have filed their taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has quite an efficient system to make paying taxes as painless as possible.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Never a pleasure, but, at least, as painless as possible.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are also doing more to communicate Government policies and programmes in a simple and clear manner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, our Pioneer Generation Ambassadors go door to door to help our Pioneers and their families better understand how they can benefit from the Pioneer Generation Package and MediShield Life by using different languages and dialects most comfortable to our Pioneers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board has added an illustrated summary in CPF members' annual statements so that we can see at one glance our own CPF contributions, account balances and transactions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: CPF Board also provides personalised financial tips on retirement planning targeted at different segments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee also asked about our plans to help our public officers do a better job at the frontline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In line with SkillsFuture, we will continue to raise the skills of all our public officers and provide them with learning and career development opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This applies to our frontline service officers as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have developed a service competency framework to spell out the skills that our frontline service officers need.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These include partnering members of the public to address concerns and working across organisations to manage cross-cutting issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have also provided additional learning and development opportunities for service staff to acquire these skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, the Civil Service College runs a suite of programmes for service staff and these service staff come from different levels of responsibility.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Some of these modules count towards a UniSIM certification programme in public sector service management.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Officers can also use these credits to count towards a minor in public sector service management from UniSIM, if they wish to pursue a degree.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This helps to raise the professionalism of the service role and provides avenues for our officers to deepen their knowledge and skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Public Service Division (PSD) is also working with agencies to develop competency-based service career paths and introduce more leadership positions for service professionals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Besides upskilling individual officers, agencies are also improving their organisational ability to improve service delivery and this includes integrating key components of service delivery, such as customer experience, data analytics and operations planning.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This helps our agencies to serve Singaporeans more effectively.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng and also Mr Ang Hin Kee asked about harassment towards public officers and the measures to protect them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Public Service is committed to providing good service to the public, based on the principle of mutual courtesy and respect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Indeed, the vast majority of the many millions of transactions between the public and our officers take place in a courteous and professional manner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, we have to take this in perspective.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is a very small proportion of the millions of interactions between public officers and members of the public every year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, we take each of these cases seriously and will take a very firm approach to those who hurt or abuse our public officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Agencies have already taken steps to protect our officers and prepare them better for their public-facing roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, officers with frontline responsibilities are trained to manage difficult situations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our agencies have also established safe work environments that encourage positive interactions with the public, for example, by installing CCTVs at service counters, assist buttons for the service staff and, for those who are on the move, body-worn cameras.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We also display service charters at many of the service counters so that the expectations that the public bring and our frontline officers have, are better matched.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Where the facts justify this, we will take legal action against those who abuse public officers in the course of their duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Protection from Harassment Act which came into effect in November 2014 provides for stiffer penalties against such perpetrators.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But I would emphasise that we will do so only when the facts of the case justify this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And we will and must continue to promote a culture of mutual courtesy and respect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng says, it is more developing this culture than laws or sanctions or body-worn cameras or CCTVs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is this culture of mutual respect and courtesy that we should make the norm in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is an important area, as we depend on science and technology to overcome our resource constraints, such as water and land.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These constraints will bite even more in the coming years once the climate change agreement takes effect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, we will have to make sure that what we do is, indeed, sustainable from a carbon emissions point of view.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will need to use technology more strategically in the next phase of Singapore's development in infrastructure, housing and transport to make Singapore a highly liveable and desirable city, to make full use of the revolution in info-comms technology to improve business efficiency and public services, and to protect our people and our country.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, I will use land-related examples today of how science and technology have played a role in our development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our geotechnical engineers built the world's first large-scale Underground Ammunition Facility, which opened in 2008, and it freed up space above ground for other uses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The professionalism and thoroughness of the analysis, design and testing by our engineers have been internationally recognised.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The safety standards developed by our engineers for underground ammunition storage have been adopted by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) as the standard.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In 2014, we opened the Jurong Rock Caverns, Southeast Asia's first commercial underground liquid hydrocarbon storage facility on Jurong Island.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There are nine storage galleries with a total capacity almost 100 times the size of this Parliament Chamber.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, each storage gallery is about 10 to 11 times the size of this Parliament chamber and it is about 130 metres under the seabed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Today, our engineers are looking to further exploit underground spaces, such as the feasibility of an underground reservoir.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Singapore Land Authority, National Research Foundation, and GovTech are working together on Virtual Singapore, a dynamic 3D city model and collaborative data platform with 3D maps of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: With a diverse range of realtime and static data, this platform will allow authorised public and private users to run simulations, plan new infrastructure, design new solutions, in line with our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will need more engineers in the Public Service to drive these efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I spoke about building up engineering capabilities across the Public Service at the Institution of Engineers in February and will provide more details today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: About 70% of these 1,000 additional engineers will support our infrastructure development needs, including transport and water systems.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The rest will support our Smart Nation efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Public agencies are also now in the process of studying their medium-term engineering manpower needs and are working towards building up a sustainable pool of engineers in key engineering clusters in the Public Service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Salaries for engineers and ICT professionals vary across different public agencies today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Some of our agencies are already paying salaries that are largely competitive with the market, while the salaries in other agencies lag significantly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will review our salaries regularly to ensure that they are competitive with the market.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In specific areas, we will pay a premium for engineers with skills that are in high demand and short supply, such as cyber forensics and malware analysts, or those with niche skills that are critical and specific to the Government but for which there may be little market demand.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But we still need them and they are critical to us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will also review the salaries of our serving engineers and raise them where needed, to ensure that public sector engineering salaries remain competitive at every job level and not just at the starting level.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, third, we will offer our engineers good learning and development opportunities to build deep technical expertise throughout their careers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will start by developing competency frameworks for engineers from seven public agencies, such as PUB and HDB, in the second half of 2016.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This framework will articulate the knowledge and skills that our public sector engineers require as they progress in their careers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our engineers can use this framework to identify their own training needs and develop expertise and mastery in specific areas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, we hope to have many more engineers of the type that Mr Liang Eng Hwa talked about – people who love their jobs, who thoroughly know their jobs, and who can serve the public very well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In addition, we will build on existing programmes that agencies have in place for technical specialists and make a more concerted effort to identify and develop engineers with deep technical expertise to take on key scientific, engineering and technical leadership positions in Ministries and public agencies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They will be given greater support in their career development and growth, for example, mentoring by senior technical experts, working on exciting interagency engineering projects, and networking across the engineering community.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Through such training opportunities and exposure, good public sector engineers will be prepared to take on positions, such as Chief Engineers, Chief Technology Officers and the like, in the Public Service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will be expanding the scope of some of the existing technical leadership positions in our agencies and creating more new ones.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These technical leaders will champion R&D efforts to develop new solutions, improve performance and service, and help build deep technical expertise in key capability areas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They will act as the bridge with industry and research partners to supplement public sector engineering expertise and help our Ministries and agencies use technology strategically for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Fourth, we will establish Centres of Excellence for key engineering knowledge clusters, building them around agencies which already have a strong base of engineering capabilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These centres will aggregate key capabilities and build deep engineering expertise in critical areas of need.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Taken together, these measures will attract more Singaporeans to take up engineering as a meaningful, fulfilling and exciting long-term career in the Public Service and deepen our public sector engineering capabilities over time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our public officers have worked closely with Singaporeans to contribute to nation-building in our first 50 years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: To ensure that the Public Service remains ready for the future, we will continue to identify key priorities early and invest in strengthening the capabilities of our officers in new and important areas, such as emerging technology, data analytics, leadership skills, service management and public engagement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Beyond skills and capabilities, our officers must have the heart and passion to do their best for Singaporeans and Singapore, to derive their satisfaction from seeing other Singaporeans happy and fulfilled.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our Public Service values of Integrity, Service and Excellence provide an anchor for our officers as they carry out their duties every day.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am confident that our public officers will continue, with your support, to work hand in hand with Singaporeans to build an even better Singapore in the future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This, the CPIB says, is testament to Singapore's continued vigilance, commitment and zero-tolerance approach in our fight against corruption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While CPIB's low caseload is one thing, it seems that, internationally, there are some doubts as to whether we have been as vigilant and intolerant towards corruption as claimed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In particular, it has been suggested that we have a certain double standard – intolerance towards corruption within Singapore, but permissiveness towards corruption committed abroad.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the main factors is Singapore's position as a global financial centre and its reputation for having strong banking secrecy laws that could shield those who have broken laws overseas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Articles have been written, mostly abroad, accusing Singapore of "asking no questions" or "turning a blind eye" to sources of funds being managed from here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since about 2009, the Government has progressively implemented regulations requiring more vigilance, increased reporting and exchange of information with other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are guided by international standards set by the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, Singapore now has in place some anti-money laundering measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But how effective are they to prevent the inflow of corrupt monies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Concerns have also been raised about locally-based firms, such as Portcullis Trustnet, which purportedly specialise in setting up offshore companies and trusts and hard-to-trace bank accounts in Singapore and other offshore financial centres.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another weakness in Singapore's fight against corruption from abroad seems to be our lack of extradition treaties with other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the Government concerned that Singapore's anti-corruption reputation has thus been eroded?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We totally agree with Ms Sylvia Lim that while our corruption numbers are low, we must continue to maintain our vigilance.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we always say, "low corruption does not necessarily mean no corruption".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The nature of corruption is a constantly evolving challenge and we must always maintain our vigilance.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our reputation for being against corruption is hard fought and hard won but that does not mean that we can let our guard down.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Member asked about our fight on the financial front.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore is well-known for our policy of zero-tolerance against corruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have a robust and comprehensive anti-corruption framework.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As an international financial centre, Singapore has an important part to play in the global effort against money laundering, including that related to corruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: MAS requires financial institutions here to put in place adequate controls to detect and deter the flow of illicit funds through Singapore's financial system.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Financial Institutions are required to report any suspicious transactions that they come across.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In addition, Singapore's Financial Intelligence Unit – the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO) – plays an important role in detecting illicit funds entering our financial system.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: STRO receives and analyses reports of suspicious transactions and other financial intelligence.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Where possible offences are detected, STRO disseminates the intelligence to relevant domestic law enforcement agencies and STRO's foreign counterparts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Such intelligence has assisted both local and foreign jurisdictions to bring corrupt persons and other criminals to justice and recover proceeds of crime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If any Member of the House has any information relating to possible acts of corruption, I would strongly urge everyone to help CPIB by providing such information for us to investigate, so that we can get to the bottom of it.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ultimately, the best test of how good we are and how good our reputation is lies in the fact whether people will put their trust in us, do business with us or place their money here.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is in our collective interest to make sure that we not only maintain our reputation but to continuously strengthen that trust for people to put their assets and intellectual property with us.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How do we grow our population so that there will always be the numbers to ensure that our Singapore identity, culture and beliefs form the nucleus of the next generation?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Low birth rate is not a problem unique to Singapore alone.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many other developed countries, too, are confronted with this issue.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Giving various cash incentives, or baby bonuses, or extended parental leave for parents may help somehow.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But we still need more babies to replace ourselves.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As a parent of three growing up children, I know what it is like starting a family and to juggle this responsibility with a career.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: To encourage young married couples to start a family, we need to adopt a holistic approach with coordinated efforts by a multi-Ministry task force.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Families with both parents working need caregiver assistance to help look after their children.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Bringing up a child needs a lot of support and there are some that are fortunate who they can turn to their parents for help.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I urge the Government to do more to assist young parents in childcare, especially in the first six years after birth.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister update the House on what is our Government's strategy towards creating a favourable environment for Singaporeans to start families and raise children?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is the offer of monetary incentives the best option?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Did the Government do any survey to find out why more couples decided to have children last year?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many other countries in this group are developed economies, which include Hong Kong, Taiwan and Korea.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, the countries with the best TFRs appear to all be the developing world, with Sub-Saharan Africa having nine of the top 10 slots, with TFR greater than six.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Are there any lessons we can learn from other countries?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There seems to be an inverse relationship between development and population growth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I wonder if there are any lessons that we can learn from developed countries that seem to have been able to deal with the TFR.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans today are sophisticated, well-educated and have diverse and ambitious aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many look forward to enjoying a good family life while building their careers as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are worthy of our support and we must do what we can to support them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some young Singaporeans find themselves struggling to balance their roles as a responsible parent and a performing employee, often compromising one for the other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, parenthood and career-building need not be mutually exclusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Beyond Government initiatives, we need a whole-of-society movement to secure a win-win outcome.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We, as a society, need to celebrate marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, the culture and structure at the workplaces need to also complement such efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, employers should promote fairer appraisal systems that do not mark down mothers or fathers because they had to be taken out of action for a few months or if they took childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Focus the appraisals on outcomes and the quality of work product.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should also continue to promote flexi-work: incentivise the use of technology to reduce the need for face time so as to enable working parents to work just as effectively out of the office.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And speaking of support for young parents, we have always been talking about infant care and childcare centres, but we know that supply is still chasing demand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Manpower in this area has also been tight and will continue to be challenging.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask if we could have a rethink about how we want to help young working parents in this aspect.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can we consider alternatives other than care centres and family support which not everyone has?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These can be experienced women or we know them as "aunties" or trained part-time caregivers who want to take care of infants and children and earn an income at the same time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These potential caregivers may be keen but have not been able to find the families who need them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government can help match demand with supply by creating an online directory to facilitate this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Interested parents who cannot secure a placement at the infant care or childcare centre can look to this platform for potential caregivers within the neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Basic profiles and credentials of these caregivers can be published in the directory.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Interested caregivers can also be offered a refresher course customised to match their educational background.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given their experience, the course need not be over an extended period and, therefore, their "time-to-market" would be shorter.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Their completion of such a course or other comparable certification, assuming they attended institutional training, can be published in the directory as part of their credentials.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Parents can browse through the directory on their own and decide for themselves who they want to engage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They can then negotiate the price privately with the caregivers listed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In essence, the directory serves as just a platform for demand to find supply.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reasons for this and, hence, the policy tools to address this are necessarily complex and multifaceted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even Japan and Switzerland are doing better at 1.4 and 1.5 respectively.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is only so much we can and should do to nudge Singaporeans to marry and have babies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps, our focus can be on encouraging those parents who do have one or two children to have more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, I think policies to ease the difficulties of having more children when one already has some, infant care and access to childcare, in particular, may be crucial.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When a family already has one or two children, the logistical issues of having a third child or fourth child tend to weigh heavily.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other countries do have programmes where the states sponsor some parents in a particular neighbourhood to provide quasi, informal child and infant care to their neighbours, as in Denmark; or sends part-time helpers to help mothers with new-borns to cope for a month or two, as in France.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope this is something we can look at seriously, taking a whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, taking time off work is considered a luxury by most working parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the Government can encourage extended family closeness by giving out grants and building more 3-Gen flats, it is definitely also important for immediate family members to spend time together and for parents to look after their child when they are sick or in need of help.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How then do we make the positives more apparent and parenthood less daunting?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, targeting costs, though key, is but one way of lowering the threshold for those considering to have children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We talked of a whole-of-Government approach to promoting innovation and a business-friendly environment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we consider a whole-of-society approach to promoting parenthood?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, at the community level, can we develop more child-friendly community spaces, for instance, indoor playgrounds, where parents can have a cup of coffee as they watch their children play, or nursing rooms and baby-changing rooms decorated to be a little haven for parents and children, with soft music and alluring hues?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Young parents can be made to feel special and not so alone in their endeavour.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have set aside resources to develop trade associations and chambers to encourage industry self-help and transformation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we can change mindsets towards parenthood, hopefully, the question will be "Why not?"

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Societal views do not help – we idolise the successful, we individualise the achiever, we are motivated to be the first to reach the finishing line, preferably alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We do not celebrate family enough, not in the same way we celebrate individual success.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If there is one thing we have learnt, money is not the motivating factor.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, I am uncomfortable even with the term "baby bonus".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The baby itself is the bonus, a bonus from a happy marriage that forms the basis for joy and hope in family life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The top-ups, bonuses if we have to call them that, help, but they can never be the motivation for having children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To support that, the whole society must undergo de-evolution, to return to our focus on the family as a core unit of the nation, that children complete us, not conflict with us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As they say, it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In metropolis Singapura, the kampung network of support has slowly faded away.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even at our workplaces, those on maternity leave are sometimes vilified, shunned and demotivated by unsupportive employers and co-workers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Motherhood, that most noble of vocations, is debased as a burden on the bottom line, a weighty problem for progress.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One employer recently complained to me: "Your zheng hu (government) keeps extending this leave, that leave.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Very soon, everyone on leave, I have to leave the business and my business will zup lup (close down)." Well, the question is: has any company actually zup lup because of pro-family leave policies?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The laws of probability are more than likely to prove otherwise.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For those who feel that this and our maternity leave are too generous, I think it bears reminding ourselves that not too long ago, our own mothers would not have had maternity benefits.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, we should advocate the impossible and dream the improbable as, in one generation, we have achieved much in changes to our pro-family policies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fathers should also be encouraged to play bigger roles not because they want to but because they should.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Charles Ballard, an American fatherhood advocate, described fatherhood as such: "Have no fear.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It isn't easy, it's the hardest thing you'll ever do and you would probably feel very, very lonely but know that you make a great difference." Fathers should not be seen just as breadwinners.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They should be encouraged to have shared parenthood responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For that to happen, society and infrastructure must change.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The worship of male machismo must be replaced by respect for fathering.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a father myself, I have faced many logistical nightmares when heading out with my boys.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have even changed nappies on my knees in the toilet for the lack of facilities for fathers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In some places, even brand new baby rooms are perpetually locked up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I ask why, the answer is, "prevent abuse".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Encourage employers to set aside proper nursing rooms for mothers, too.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But this most natural of instincts seems to sometimes illicit fear and revulsion even amongst members of the public.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We, on the one hand, allow the disgraceful debasement of the female body and yet, we cry foul when half a bosom is exposed by a nursing mother.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we spend billions on encouraging couples to have babies, why do we not do something for those already conceived?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It felt like that one piece of the puzzle that would have made this mosaic complete was missing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I will be the first to say that, along the way, with joy comes responsibilities and lots and lots of hard work.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would not give that up for anything in this world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We will regret not having spent enough time with our children and not the other way around.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also welcomed more than 33,000 Jubilee babies last year as we celebrated SG50.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Government share its strategy towards creating a conducive environment for Singaporeans to get married and have children?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One area which the Government can look further into is housing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think the waiting period for a BTO flat is too long.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our young Singaporeans getting married at a later age, the child-bearing years are also getting shorter.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Government allocate more flats to this scheme, especially in mature estates, so that couples can choose to stay close to their parents living in the same town or near to established infant-care centres?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think there must be a balance in the approach so that as we provide support for Singaporeans to go for marriage and parenthood, we do not overlook career aspirations and heartware, such as better family-friendly environment and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I agree with the hon Member, Mr Melvin Yong, about the waiting time for a new BTO flat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I strongly support the reduction of the waiting time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second point I want to raise is that recently, I have resident mothers who approached me to give feedback about the inability to carry baby prams or strollers on board buses with several kids and groceries in tow, and I have personally experienced it with my children as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can PMO look into a whole-of-Government approach to improve family-friendly environment and services in our public transport system in the hope of enticing more young parents who have children with ease of family travel and reduce the logistical pains of parenthood whilst on public transport?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For career aspirations, how can we walk the talk to eliminate discrimination in the workplace, in particular, for expectant mothers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and PMO explore the possibility to ensure that the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) continues to have teeth to effectively weed out workplace discrimination and advocate fair employment, in particular, for expectant mothers, in the workplace?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, fellow Members of Parliament, the Government has been enhancing policies to increase the birth rate, including helping singles to find life partners, housing, encouraging procreation, childcare, work-life balance, getting husbands and wives to share responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, all possible ways and means have been used to address the issue of our country's ageing population and declining birth rate.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On the relationship between population and a nation's strength, I would like to share a story from ancient China.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: During the Song Dynasty, there was a small kingdom called Western Xia, or 西夏.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The soldiers were valiant and good at fighting, winning numerous battles against the Greater Song.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, Western Xia, despite having a strong army with great fighting spirit, ultimately had to make peace with the Greater Song because of its small population and lack of manpower.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This story illustrates how a small, but tough nation lost because of its shrinking population, reminding us that the size of Singapore's population and its demographic structure is related to its economic development, social stability and national defence.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The strong Western Xia survived for close to 200 years and, similarly, as a small nation surrounded by bigger nations, how long can Singapore survive?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Having just celebrated 50 years of nation-building, we are beginning our journey towards the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If we are unable to solve the issues of an ageing population, businesses would eventually face a more severe manpower challenge.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, supporting the country's population policy would mean supporting the sustainable development of businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, businesses do face difficulties during the implementation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: There is a conflict between implementing lean management, increasing productivity and promoting family-friendly and flexible working arrangements.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, on the topic of increasing the birth rate, how is the Government going to communicate even more effectively with the citizens?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We should handle the population issue with the same perseverance we have in resolving the water issue.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes: "Everyone is responsible for the rise and fall of the country".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Marriage and parenthood should be, from now on, a national concern.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This should be an important pillar in supporting family-centric workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But first, let me address some concerns on paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Senor Minister of State Josephine Teo has said that the Government will give firms time to adjust and phase in the second week of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This might be due to a combination of manpower constraints and the mindsets of workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will the Government help our young fathers deal with such constraints to improve the consumption rate of paternity leave?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we promote and share best practices?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Broad legislation, such as extended paternity leave is an important signpost of the Government's intent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, we should also consider alternative tripartite frameworks to catalyse the proliferation of family-centric workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, telecommuting will work quite well for office-based workers but less so for production-based ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mothers who work shifts will find it quite challenging to get on board the FWA journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Taking a sectoral approach, the Government can develop targeted measures for companies, unions or trade associations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will be akin to ICT being used as a means to catalyse and spread innovation under the industry transformation programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With similar companies grouped together, the tripartite partners can implement a flexible career system for mothers in the first year of their maternity in this system, for example, a mother on workshifts can find alternative office hour careers with the companies, unions or trade associations supported by the Government, of course.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even industries with civic childcare centres catering to the working hours of the specific industry could be possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government consider developing sectoral solutions with our tripartite partners?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Family-centric workplaces are possible but it requires both legislation and the inventiveness and boldness of our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, the sectoral manpower plans (SMPs) being developed by the sectoral tripartite committees (STCs) should value family-centric work practices as a core element in developing human capital.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government work with STCs to incorporate family-centric strategies within the SMPs?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Then they would decide whether or not to have children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once they have had a child, they would then decide whether or not to have more children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These three key decision-points in a couple's life also correspond to three different demographic groups, each of which, in my opinion, requires a different approach and strategy in terms of encouraging them to have more children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the reality is that the process of raising a child can also be a challenging one at times, especially for first-time parents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Expenses aside, there are times when first-time parents are grappling with new experiences that can seem rather stressful.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I feel that perhaps more could be done to enhance the entire ecosystem to provide more holistic support for parents, especially during pregnancy and in the first year after birth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, for those who have made the choice to have children, I believe that we can certainly help to make the child-raising experience a smoother and more enjoyable one.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would then have a positive effect on parents' decision to have more children in the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To echo what my colleague Ms Sun Xueling said, "Children, why not?" Or better still, "Children, of course!" I would thus like to ask NPTD what can be done to foster more supportive social norms and positive mindsets towards marriage and parenthood in the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think we all agree, Madam, that Singapore needs to have talent from all over the world to benefit our economy and support our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I agree that many of these foreigners add to the richness and diversity of our society as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our forefathers were immigrants and we continue to see new communities join our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have seen differences in culture and practices from among the new groups and even among Singaporeans born in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Through the Ethnic Integration Policy, the Government sought to address the emergence of enclaves and helped people of various racial and religious backgrounds to integrate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Children from a particular estate largely went to the schools in the vicinity, thus helping to cement their common experiences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They may not have the opportunity to interact on a daily basis with other Singaporeans and do not share similar experiences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This means that we can have children who have lived in Singapore but have very little common experiences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must, therefore, be conscious of the challenges in promoting organic integration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, are there more ways we can create platforms for open and candid discussions about our differences and learn how to celebrate and embrace our diversity?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If I may, in the course of my presentation, I will also screen some slides, Madam.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is near to the end of the debate and I started to reflect.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On numerous occasions during this debate, Members spoke about the "Singaporean Core".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clearly, it is something we all care deeply about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the work of NPTD has very much to do with strengthening our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In promoting marriage and parenthood, we are growing the Singaporean Core from within.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Through efforts to keep in touch with Overseas Singaporeans and catalyse integration of new citizens, we aim to keep Singapore cohesive and open, to become stronger as one even as we spread our wings and as we welcome new members to our Singaporean family to supplement and expand the core.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members know by now that I would very much like to share some thoughts on how we can strengthen support for marriage and parenthood because it is of vital importance that we can grow the Singaporean Core from within.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It shows how Singaporeans are increasingly mobile and welcomed by employers and educational institutions internationally.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One interesting result is that we now have more "Singapore Citizens by Descent".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This refers to children born overseas to fathers or mothers who are Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The only difference with Singaporeans by birth is that they are born overseas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the first half of this decade, the number was around 1,400 annually, on average.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it is a 15% increase over 10 years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Overseas Singaporean Unit (OSU) reaches out to our Overseas Singaporeans to connect them back to Singapore, through nurturing close-knit, vibrant Singaporean communities overseas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Whenever Ministers have official duties overseas, we make it a point to catch up with our Overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Here is a picture of Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean in Brazil.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It surprised me that there were so many Singaporeans in Brazil.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And this is a picture of Overseas Singaporeans in Copenhagen, whom I met in March.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we must make an effort to keep in touch.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, we must make an effort to help all citizens, the new and the not-so-new, to gel as one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Members know, immigration helps us to top up and improve the age balance in our citizen population.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our aim is to prevent our citizen population from shrinking.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What that means is that we have kept a calibrated pace of immigration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The population of PRs remained stable – 29,955 new PRs were granted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By the time they are conferred citizenship, most new citizens have been living here for years and many have also established family ties with other Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, one reason Singapore feels like home to them is the openness and sense of welcome that many Singaporeans generously extend to newcomers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not surprising because in many Singaporean families, it is quite common nowadays to have in-laws who are foreigners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More couples these days have wedding receptions in two or more countries because that is where the family networks extend.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nonetheless, the Government must do its part to help new citizens deepen their sense of belonging.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, since 2011, all new citizens have been asked to participate in the Singapore Citizenship Journey.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a programme that reinforces Singapore's values and norms and facilitates further involvement in the community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It also properly welcomes new citizens into the Singaporean family.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: New citizens need to get involved in all aspects of local life, such as learning to speak local languages, and, some say, Singlish also; interacting with their neighbours; adapting to local behavioural norms; and taking an interest in issues that concern their fellow citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most important of all, they must understand our roots as a multiracial and multicultural society, where each community enjoys our common space and interacts respectfully with one another.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, they must imbibe it and make it part of their identity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, Singaporeans have an important contribution to make.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides reaching out to new citizens and strengthening cohesion, we should stay open as a society to people of diverse backgrounds, which both Mr Darryl David and Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It goes hand in hand with being a society that is open to new ideas and innovation and capable of positive change and the capacity for excellence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The open-mindedness of young Singaporeans gives us reasons to be hopeful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Sometime last year, a group of undergraduates at the Nanyang Technological University's (NTU's) Wee Kim Wee School of Communications started a campaign with a simple yet inviting slogan "Come, Let's Eat".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This initiative brought a great diversity of people together through the universal language of food, one language that we all understand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singaporeans shared our local flavours at cooking classes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And the foreigners reciprocated by hosting local foodies at restaurants serving their hometown cuisines.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the signature event which they named "Global Potluck", 80 participants tasted dishes, such as Turkish meatballs, German potato salad and, of course, our very own "popiah" and "satay".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Although the campaign lasted just a few months, participants made new friends and still keep in touch through social media.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These ground-up initiatives are modest but sincere efforts by individuals and groups to keep Singapore an open society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government provides support through the Community Integration Fund.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it is really the passion for Singapore, the conviction that we have something special to share, the spirit of generosity and openness that have motivated the organisers to keep the projects going.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last year, it was the slowest since the Global Financial Crisis of 2009.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat and Manpower Minister Lim Swee Say have spoken about the support that the Government is giving to businesses to ease the crunch.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister Lim also outlined the many measures that MOM is introducing to help Singaporeans adapt and grow.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One such example is the Human Capital Partnership (HCP) with the "triple strong" companies to nurture local talents into regional and global talents through skills transfers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These efforts are aimed at strengthening the Singaporean Core in our workforce so that we can better manage the need to supplement our workforce and, as much as possible, keep them to specific job roles, such as those requiring skills that are hard to find among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, MOM is stepping up efforts to build a strong Singaporean Core in the workforce and to strengthen our global competitiveness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, through tightening work pass applications for employers who are identified to be "triple weak".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, through the SkillsFuture initiative led by Minister Ong Ye Kung, we will help Singaporeans stay relevant and participate meaningfully in the workforce at every stage of their lives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our vision must be a Singapore that is cohesive and open, where Singaporeans feel a sense of connectedness wherever they are in the world, confident to move forward as one and, at the same time, have the capacity to welcome new additions to our family, whether for a period of time or for good.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such a Singapore will be a worthy place for each one of us to nurture our families in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But first, let me thank Mr Thomas Chua for sharing with us the story of Western Xia (西夏).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He has very poignantly reminded us that marriage and parenthood, birth rates and population are, ultimately, about economic vitality, even our defence capacity and, in the long term, our nation's survival.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The question on Members' minds is, naturally, can we boost our TFR further?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is not a trivial question, as I explained in an Op-Ed for The Sunday Times recently.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But besides researching other countries' experiences, I have taken a few months to consult people, including parents, some with a few kids and others with many, whether they are young or grown-up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have consulted young people who have yet to date or marry and I have also asked scholars who have studied the subject for years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The short answer to this question is, yes, I believe our TFR can go up, but if and only if the whole of Singapore society gets behind this effort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am optimistic because aspirations for marriage and parenthood remain very strong.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, there is no silver bullet, no single policy intervention, not even a set of policy interventions that will boost TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
